messages.content: I want to develop long-tail image recognition that preserves rare-class accuracy when predictive background correlations reverse, without target-domain labels. How should I state the goal precisely?

The goal is to improve recognition of rare classes under background reversals without relying on target-domain labels. Specifically, bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy should be at least 5 percentage points higher than an empirical risk minimization baseline under those reversals. At the same time, top-quintile class macro-accuracy should remain within 1 percentage point of that baseline, using identical training data.
What does the background reversal condition add to the goal?

It makes the goal about more than accuracy in a long-tail setting. The concern is that a background can be predictive of a class in one setting but point the other way when the correlation reverses. The rare-class improvement is required under that reversal condition, rather than merely when the familiar background–class association persists.
So is it enough to improve rare-class accuracy in general?

No. A general rare-class improvement would not, by itself, establish the stated target. The specified comparison is bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy against empirical risk minimization under background reversals, with an improvement of 5 percentage points. The top-quintile constraint is part of the goal as well.
Why distinguish the bottom and top quintiles?

They express two requirements that must hold together. The bottom-quintile measure captures the intended gain for the rare-class end of the long tail. The top-quintile measure limits how far performance for the classes at the other end can move from the empirical risk minimization baseline. The goal is not simply to increase one aggregate accuracy number.
What exactly is class macro-accuracy doing here?

It treats class-level accuracy as the quantity being averaged within the specified group of classes. Thus, bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy refers to the average across classes in that quintile, rather than an accuracy dominated by whichever classes contribute the most individual images. The same reading applies to the top quintile.
Is the rare-class improvement relative or in percentage points?

It is an absolute difference of 5 percentage points over the empirical risk minimization baseline, not a 5 percent relative increase. The wording specifies percentage points for both thresholds: 5 for the bottom-quintile improvement and 1 for the top-quintile closeness requirement.
Could I focus entirely on the bottom-quintile gain and treat the top-quintile number as background context?

No. Keeping top-quintile class macro-accuracy within 1 percentage point of the empirical risk minimization baseline is an explicit requirement. The desired rare-class gain and the top-quintile constraint need to be considered together; meeting only the bottom-quintile threshold would not fully express the goal.
Does “within 1 percentage point” mean the top-quintile accuracy has to improve?

Not as stated. “Within 1 percentage point of that baseline” specifies closeness to the empirical risk minimization result. It does not require a top-quintile improvement. The important distinction is between that closeness requirement and the directional requirement that bottom-quintile accuracy improve by 5 percentage points.
And what does “using identical training data” constrain?

It makes the comparison with empirical risk minimization a like-for-like one with respect to training data. The bottom-quintile gain and top-quintile closeness should not be attributed to one side having different training data. The goal does not, however, specify a particular training procedure or recognition method.
Does “without target-domain labels” mean I should assume anything else about the target domain?

No additional assumption is stated. The approach must not rely on target-domain labels. That condition alone does not specify whether any unlabeled target-domain images are available, nor does it prescribe how the approach handles the reversal. Those details are outside the stated goal.
Is empirical risk minimization a proposed method here or just the comparator?

It is the named baseline for the two accuracy comparisons. The desired long-tail recognition approach is measured against empirical risk minimization under background reversals: at least 5 percentage points better on bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy, while staying within 1 percentage point on top-quintile class macro-accuracy with identical training data.
Would a strong bottom-quintile gain make the top-quintile condition less important?

The stated goal does not trade one requirement away for a larger gain on the other. It calls for preserving performance at the top end while improving the bottom end under background reversals. A bottom-quintile gain should therefore be read alongside, not in place of, the top-quintile comparison.
Can we say the approach already preserves rare-class accuracy under reversals?

Not yet. This is a development goal with numerical success conditions, not a report of an achieved result. It says what the approach should do; it does not state that a method has been selected, evaluated, or shown to meet either threshold.
I want a concise version that still includes every constraint.

Develop long-tail image recognition without target-domain labels that, under predictive background-correlation reversals, improves bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy by at least 5 percentage points over empirical risk minimization while keeping top-quintile class macro-accuracy within 1 percentage point of that baseline, using identical training data.

For that goal, I propose training a class-balanced tail adapter using self-supervised masks and background swaps within the training set, while distilling head logits from an empirical risk minimization teacher. Can you unpack the proposal?

It combines a tail-focused adaptation step with two ways of constraining what the model learns. The class-balanced tail adapter is intended to give rare classes attention. Self-supervised masks and within-training-set background swaps provide a way to train against reliance on the existing class–background associations. Distilling head logits from an empirical risk minimization (ERM) teacher is intended to retain the teacher’s behavior on head classes. These are proposed training components, not an established result.
What does “class-balanced” mean in this description?

It says the tail adapter’s training should account for class imbalance rather than letting the more frequent classes dominate by default. The proposal does not specify the exact balancing rule or how the adapter is implemented, so those details should remain open.
Why call it a tail adapter instead of just saying to retrain the recognition model?

“Tail adapter” expresses the proposed focus: adapting recognition for the rare-class end of the long tail. It does not, by itself, say which parts of a model are changed or held fixed. The separate head-logit distillation component reflects the need to attend to head-class behavior as well.
How do the masks fit with the background swaps?

Conceptually, masks can help distinguish image regions relevant to a swap from the regions to be retained. The proposal specifically calls for self-supervised masks and background swaps drawn from the training set. It does not specify a mask-generation method, require perfect masks, or define an exact swapping procedure.
Does “self-supervised” mean the masks are target-domain labels in another form?

No. The proposal calls for self-supervised masks, not target-domain labels. That distinction matters because the goal is to handle predictive background-correlation reversals without target-domain labels. The proposal does not make a further claim about what target-domain data, if any, is available.
Why insist that the backgrounds be swapped within the training set?

That is an explicit boundary of the proposal: the swaps use backgrounds from the training set. The idea is to vary the background associated with an image during training without introducing a new source of labeled target-domain examples. It does not specify how swap partners are selected.
Are the swaps meant to recreate the exact reversal the model will encounter?

The proposal does not claim that they recreate an exact target-domain reversal. Their proposed role is to make training less dependent on a particular predictive background association. Whether that is sufficient under background reversals remains something to assess against the stated accuracy requirements.
What does it mean to distill the head logits from the ERM teacher?

It means using the empirical risk minimization teacher’s output scores for head classes as a reference during training. In this proposal, that reference is a way to discourage the tail-focused adaptation from changing head-class behavior too much. The statement does not prescribe a distillation loss, a weight for it, or a guarantee that head-class accuracy will stay within the required range.
So the ERM teacher has two roles: a training reference and the comparison baseline?

The proposal names an ERM teacher as the source of head logits for distillation. The goal also names empirical risk minimization as the accuracy baseline. Those roles are related, but the proposal should not be read as proof that distilling from the teacher will meet either comparison. Performance still has to be judged against the baseline under the stated conditions.
Would distilling head logits interfere with the rare-class improvement?

It could create a tension: the adapter is meant to improve tail-class recognition, while distillation encourages it to retain the ERM teacher’s head-class outputs. The proposal combines them in pursuit of both requirements, but does not establish how that tension resolves or specify a trade-off setting.
Is the head-logit part meant to replace the top-quintile requirement?

No. Head-logit distillation is a proposed training component, whereas the top-quintile requirement is an outcome criterion: top-quintile class macro-accuracy must remain within 1 percentage point of the ERM baseline using identical training data. Distillation may be intended to help with that criterion, but it is not itself evidence that the criterion has been met.
And the masks and swaps do not automatically establish the bottom-quintile result either, right?

Right. They are proposed ways to address reliance on backgrounds. The required result remains a 5-percentage-point improvement in bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy over ERM under background reversals. The proposal does not report that result.
Could I describe this simply as augmenting the training set with swapped backgrounds?

That would capture only one component. The full proposal is to train a class-balanced tail adapter, use self-supervised masks and within-training-set background swaps, and distill head logits from an ERM teacher. Leaving out the adapter or distillation would change what has been proposed.
Does the proposal require collecting extra images or labels?

It specifies swaps within the training set and does not call for target-domain labels. It does not state a need for additional images or labels. For comparison with the goal’s ERM baseline, the identical-training-data condition remains important; the proposal does not authorize assuming a larger labeled training set.
What should I avoid claiming when I explain the proposed benefit?

Avoid saying that the method already works under background reversals, that its masks reliably isolate every relevant region, or that ERM-teacher distillation guarantees top-quintile preservation. It is accurate to say the proposal is designed to pursue rare-class robustness while constraining changes to head-class behavior. Whether it reaches the 5-percentage-point bottom-quintile gain and the 1-percentage-point top-quintile limit is not established here.
Can you give me a compact statement of the whole proposal without turning its intended effects into results?

Propose training a class-balanced tail adapter with self-supervised masks and within-training-set background swaps to address dependence on predictive backgrounds, while distilling head logits from an ERM teacher to help preserve head-class behavior. This is a proposed route toward the long-tail recognition goal, not a claim that the accuracy thresholds have been achieved.
Do self-supervised masks preserve rare-class object cues when backgrounds are swapped, or could they erase features needed for recognition?

That is an open question. A mask could help keep the object separate from the background being swapped, but only if it retains the features the recognizer needs. Because the masks are self-supervised, the proposal alone does not establish that they preserve those features, especially for rare classes.
What would count as an object cue in this question?

An object cue is visual information that helps distinguish the object’s class. The concern is not limited to whether a mask keeps a recognizable central region: it is whether it keeps enough of the distinguishing information for rare-class recognition after the background changes. The node does not specify which cues matter for any particular class.
Could a swap make an image look clean while still removing something important?

Yes, in principle. A visually plausible swapped image would not by itself show that every recognition-relevant feature survived. The mask might omit part of the object or otherwise separate the retained and swapped regions in a way that changes the information available to the recognizer. That is a possibility raised by the question, not a finding about these masks.
So the uncertainty is about the mask, not just whether the new background is different?

Both matter to the setup, but this question focuses on what the mask preserves during the swap. Changing the background is the intended intervention; inadvertently losing rare-class object cues would be a different change. If those happen together, an apparent response to the swap could be hard to interpret as a response to background alone.
Is it fair to say self-supervision makes the masks unreliable?

That would go further than the question supports. Self-supervision does not establish either reliability or unreliability here. The precise issue is whether the resulting masks preserve the object features needed for rare-class recognition when they are used for background swaps.
Why emphasize rare classes rather than asking only whether object cues survive overall?

Because the intended benefit concerns rare-class accuracy. A mask can appear adequate in a broad sense yet still leave uncertainty about cues needed to distinguish classes at the rare end of the long tail. The question asks whether the proposed swapping step protects those cues, rather than assuming that an object-looking region is necessarily sufficient.
Could the mask retain some object information but not enough for recognition?

Yes. Preservation is not necessarily all-or-nothing. A retained region might still depict the object while omitting a feature that matters for distinguishing its class. Conversely, the question does not establish that such omission actually occurs; it identifies a risk that needs to remain separate from the intended effect of changing backgrounds.
Does preserving the object mean the background swap cannot hurt rare-class recognition?

No. Even if a mask preserves the relevant object cues, the recognizer’s response to a changed background is still an open matter. This question is narrower: whether the masking and swapping process itself keeps the information needed for recognition, or instead erases some of it.
How does this relate to the proposed tail adapter?

The tail adapter is proposed to improve recognition for rare classes, and the masked background swaps are part of its proposed training. If those swaps remove needed rare-class cues, they could work against that aim rather than simply reducing reliance on background correlations. The question does not say that this happens or that the adapter resolves it.
Would head-logit distillation answer the mask question?

Not by itself. Distilling head logits from the ERM teacher is another component of the proposal. It does not establish that self-supervised masks preserve features needed to recognize rare classes after a background swap.
Can I phrase the concern without implying that the masks have already failed?

Yes: “When self-supervised masks are used for within-training-set background swaps, do they retain the object cues required for rare-class recognition, or might they inadvertently erase those cues?” That keeps both possibilities open and does not turn the concern into a reported result.
And the distinction I should keep in mind is between removing background information and removing recognition information?

Exactly. The proposed swap aims to change background information. The unresolved question is whether the mask allows that change while preserving the object information rare-class recognition needs. Those should not be treated as the same operation merely because they occur in the same altered image.

I have a hypothesis about the mask concern: masks retaining at least 90% of the foreground should enable background swaps to lift tail macro-accuracy by at least 5 points over ERM, with no more than a 1-point head loss. Does that state it accurately?

Yes. It is a conditional prediction: if the masks retain ≥90% of the foreground, the swaps should enable tail macro-accuracy to rise by ≥5 percentage points over the empirical risk minimization (ERM) baseline, while head accuracy loses ≤1 percentage point. It addresses the concern that masking might remove information needed for recognition, but it does not establish that foreground retention is sufficient or that either accuracy threshold has been achieved.
Why does the hypothesis put a threshold on foreground retention?

The threshold makes the proposed link more specific. The hypothesis is not merely that background swaps help; it predicts the desired tail gain and limited head loss when the masks keep at least 90% of the foreground. That retained-foreground condition is meant to speak to whether the swaps leave the object available for recognition.
Does retaining 90% of the foreground mean retaining 90% of the rare-class cues?

Not necessarily. Foreground retention describes how much foreground remains, whereas recognition depends on which information remains. A mask could retain a large proportion of the foreground yet omit a small, distinctive part. That is why the ≥90% condition is a hypothesis about what should be sufficient, not proof that the needed rare-class cues survive.
Then is 90% a demonstrated cutoff?
No. In this node, ≥90% is the stated condition of the hypothesis. There is no reported result showing that this value is a cutoff at which swaps become effective, or that masks below it cannot work.
What exactly is predicted to produce the accuracy gain—the masks or the swaps?

The prediction concerns their combination: masks that retain ≥90% of the foreground should enable background swaps to lift tail macro-accuracy. The masks are not claimed to improve accuracy on their own. Their proposed role is to let the background change without erasing too much of what belongs to the foreground.
Is “should enable” stronger than saying the swaps might help?

It is a definite prediction, but still a hypothesis. It says that under the stated foreground-retention condition, the swaps are expected to achieve the specified accuracy pattern. It should not be rewritten as a completed observation such as “the swaps lifted tail macro-accuracy.”
How should I read the ≥5-point tail figure?

It means a tail macro-accuracy gain of at least 5 percentage points over ERM, not a relative increase of 5 percent. The comparison is to the ERM baseline; the hypothesis does not supply an actual accuracy value for either system.
And does the ≤1-point head loss require head accuracy to drop?

No. It caps a loss at 1 percentage point; it does not predict that a loss must occur. Head accuracy could have no loss and still satisfy that part of the hypothesis. The wording is about limiting degradation while pursuing the tail gain.
Would a 5-point tail gain alone support the whole hypothesis?

No. The predicted pattern has both parts: tail macro-accuracy must improve by at least 5 points over ERM, and head loss must be no more than 1 point. The ≥90% foreground-retention condition is also part of the hypothesis, rather than an optional detail.
Is this an answer to the earlier question of whether the masks erase needed object features?

It offers a testable answer in the form of a hypothesis, not a settled answer. It proposes that retaining ≥90% of the foreground should leave enough information for swaps to produce the stated tail gain without more than a 1-point head loss. The original concern remains meaningful because the proportion retained does not, by itself, identify which recognition-relevant features were kept.
Could I say that if a mask reaches 90%, it has preserved the object?

You could say it meets the hypothesis’s foreground-retention condition. Saying it has preserved all object cues needed for recognition would be stronger. The difference matters here: the hypothesis links high foreground retention to a predicted performance outcome, but does not assert that the retained area contains every important cue.
Does this change the background-reversal goal or replace the proposed tail adapter?

No. It narrows in on one uncertainty within the proposed masked background swaps: whether enough foreground is retained for the swaps to help tail recognition without an excessive head loss. It does not specify a different adapter or report that the broader goal under background reversals has been met.
Can you put the hypothesis and its uncertainty together in one careful sentence?

The hypothesis is that self-supervised masks retaining ≥90% of the foreground should allow background swaps to improve tail macro-accuracy by ≥5 percentage points over ERM with ≤1 percentage point of head loss, although foreground retention alone does not establish that all rare-class recognition cues are preserved or that those accuracy outcomes occur.

To examine whether the masks keep what rare-class recognition needs, I plan to audit mask retention against source-validation segmentation, then compare filtered versus unfiltered background swaps on LT-BackgroundFlip tail and head macro-accuracy, without target labels. Can you unpack that plan?

The plan has two linked parts. First, use source-validation segmentation as a reference for auditing how much foreground the self-supervised masks retain. Second, compare the tail and head macro-accuracy associated with filtered swaps and unfiltered swaps on LT-BackgroundFlip. Together, those steps are meant to examine both what the masks retain and what happens to recognition when swaps are filtered. This is a planned audit and comparison, not a reported result.
Why audit retention separately from measuring accuracy?

They answer different questions. The retention audit examines the masks themselves against the source-validation segmentation reference. The macro-accuracy comparison examines recognition outcomes for filtered versus unfiltered swaps. An accuracy difference alone would not tell you how much foreground the masks kept, while a retention measurement alone would not tell you whether the resulting swaps helped recognition.
Does source-validation segmentation mean using target-domain segmentation to decide which masks pass?

No. The stated reference is source-validation segmentation. The plan does not call for target-domain segmentation or target labels to audit mask retention. Keeping that distinction clear matters because the comparison is intended to proceed without target labels.
What does “against source-validation segmentation” establish?

It identifies what the masks are compared with for the retention audit: segmentation on source-validation examples. It does not, by itself, say that the self-supervised masks preserve every feature needed for recognition. The audit can address how well they retain foreground relative to that reference; the separate accuracy comparison addresses the recognition consequence.
If a mask retains most of the segmented foreground, can I conclude it retained the rare-class cues?

Not solely from that measurement. Foreground retention describes how much of the reference foreground is kept, not necessarily whether a small but important distinguishing feature survives. That is part of the reason to pair the mask audit with tail macro-accuracy rather than treating retained area as a complete answer to the recognition question.
What is being compared when you say filtered versus unfiltered swaps?

The comparison is between swaps that have been filtered and swaps that have not, with tail and head macro-accuracy examined on LT-BackgroundFlip. The plan does not specify the filtering rule, its threshold, or the outcome of the comparison. Those should not be filled in as though they were already decided or observed.
Would it be accurate to describe the unfiltered swaps as the baseline?

They are the comparison condition for the filtered swaps in this plan. Calling them a comparison condition avoids confusing them with the empirical risk minimization baseline used in the broader accuracy goal. The plan names a filtered-versus-unfiltered swap comparison; it does not say that those two conditions exhaust every possible baseline comparison.
Why look at both tail and head macro-accuracy instead of only the tail number?

The tail measure speaks to whether the swaps are compatible with rare-class recognition, which motivated the mask question. The head measure shows whether any tail-side change coincides with a change at the head end. Looking at both avoids describing a tail result in isolation when the long-tail objective also cares about retaining head-class performance.
Does the plan predict that filtering will improve tail accuracy?

No outcome is stated in the plan. It proposes comparing filtered and unfiltered swaps so their tail and head macro-accuracy can be examined. An improvement, no difference, or a decline would be a result of that comparison, not something already established by planning it.
What role does LT-BackgroundFlip have here?

LT-BackgroundFlip is the named setting on which the filtered and unfiltered swaps are to be compared using tail and head macro-accuracy. The plan does not specify further details about its construction, labels, or evaluation protocol, so the name should not be used to infer those details.
Could the mask audit alone settle whether the swaps erase features needed for recognition?

It can inform that concern, but it cannot settle it alone. Comparing masks with source-validation segmentation addresses foreground retention. Whether filtered or unfiltered swaps affect recognition is what the LT-BackgroundFlip macro-accuracy comparison is intended to examine. Neither step should be described as a completed answer before the audit and comparison have been carried out.
Does the phrase “without target labels” apply only to training the adapter?

The plan says to conduct this audit and comparison without target labels; it does not limit that phrase to the adapter. In particular, it names source-validation segmentation—not target-domain labels—as the mask-audit reference. It does not spell out every detail of how the LT-BackgroundFlip accuracy scores would be obtained.
But can macro-accuracy be computed from entirely unlabeled predictions?

No. An accuracy calculation requires a way to determine whether predictions are correct. The plan's “without target labels” condition should not be taken to mean that unlabeled predictions alone yield macro-accuracy. The node leaves the scoring arrangement unspecified, so it is best not to invent one or claim that target labels are used to train, filter, or select the approach.
Should I say that the source-validation audit determines which swaps are filtered?

The plan links a mask-retention audit with a filtered-versus-unfiltered comparison, but it does not state the precise rule connecting the audit to filtering. You can say the audit is relevant to assessing the filtering idea. You should not present a particular cutoff or selection procedure as specified by this plan.
How do I keep the source-validation audit and the LT-BackgroundFlip comparison distinct in one sentence?

You could say: “Audit self-supervised mask retention against source-validation segmentation, and separately compare filtered with unfiltered background swaps on LT-BackgroundFlip using tail and head macro-accuracy, without target labels.” That preserves the distinct reference for the audit and the named setting and measures for the swap comparison, while leaving their outcomes open.
And what is the question those two parts jointly address?

They jointly address whether the masks retain foreground when used for background swaps and whether filtering those swaps makes a difference to tail and head recognition. The audit speaks to retained foreground; the macro-accuracy comparison speaks to performance. Neither part alone warrants claiming that rare-class object cues have been preserved or erased.

I’m moving to the activity: audit masks against source-validation segmentation for at least 90% foreground retention, train filtered and unfiltered adapters plus an identical-data ERM baseline, and score tail and head macro-accuracy on LT-BackgroundFlip. How do these pieces fit together?

The audit checks whether the self-supervised masks meet the ≥90% foreground-retention condition, using source-validation segmentation as the reference. Training the filtered and unfiltered adapters provides the two swap conditions to compare. Training an empirical risk minimization (ERM) baseline on identical training data provides the reference for accuracy differences. Scoring tail and head macro-accuracy on LT-BackgroundFlip then addresses the predicted tail gain and limited head loss. The activity specifies what to do, not what the scores turn out to be.
Does the segmentation audit measure accuracy?

No. It measures mask retention against the source-validation segmentation reference. Tail and head macro-accuracy are separate recognition measures obtained from scoring on LT-BackgroundFlip. Keeping those measurements distinct matters: retaining foreground and recognizing classes are related questions, but they are not the same measurement.
Is ≥90% the standard for the audit, or an accuracy result?
It is the foreground-retention threshold being audited. It is not an observed retention rate and not an accuracy score. The activity does not report how many masks, if any, meet it.
Should I describe the filtered adapter as using exactly the masks that pass the ≥90% audit?

Not from this description alone. The activity names an audit for ≥90% retention and training of filtered and unfiltered adapters, but it does not spell out the filtering rule or state exactly how audit findings determine which swaps are included. It is safe to describe the conditions as filtered versus unfiltered without inventing that rule.
Why train an unfiltered adapter as well as a filtered one?

It provides a direct comparison for the filtering aspect of the background swaps. If their LT-BackgroundFlip tail or head macro-accuracy differs, the comparison can show the performance difference between the two training conditions. The activity does not predict the direction or size of that difference.
What does the ERM run add that the filtered-versus-unfiltered comparison does not?

The adapter comparison addresses whether filtering makes a difference relative to unfiltered swaps. The identical-data ERM run supplies the baseline needed to express accuracy changes over ERM, including the hypothesized ≥5-percentage-point tail gain and ≤1-percentage-point head loss. Those are different comparisons, so neither should be silently substituted for the other.
When you say identical-data ERM, do you mean ERM has to receive the same swapped images as the adapters?

The stated constraint is identical training data for the ERM comparison; it does not specify that ERM uses the adapters’ swap transformations. Filtered and unfiltered swap training can differ as training conditions without implying that the underlying comparison uses different training datasets. The activity does not provide a more detailed data-handling protocol.
Are we scoring all three trained systems on LT-BackgroundFlip?

That is the natural reading of training filtered and unfiltered adapters and identical-data ERM while scoring LT-BackgroundFlip tail and head macro-accuracy: the scores allow comparisons among the adapter conditions and against ERM. No scores or rankings are supplied in the activity.
What would those scores tell us about the mask hypothesis?

Together with the retention audit, they let us examine its two parts: whether masks meet the ≥90% foreground condition and whether the swap-based adapter attains the predicted tail gain over ERM without more than a 1-point head loss. The scores alone would not demonstrate which object cues a mask preserved, and meeting the retention threshold alone would not demonstrate the predicted accuracy outcome.
Does “head loss of no more than 1 point” mean I should score only the tail classes if the head result looks fine?

No. The activity explicitly calls for both tail and head macro-accuracy on LT-BackgroundFlip. A tail score is needed to assess the proposed gain; a head score is needed to assess any head-side loss relative to ERM. Neither can stand in for the other.
Should the 5-point gain be calculated against the unfiltered adapter or against ERM?

The hypothesized ≥5-point tail gain is over ERM. The unfiltered adapter is the comparison for the filtered adapter, not the reference named in that gain threshold. All of these differences should be expressed in percentage points of the relevant macro-accuracy, rather than as relative percentages.
Does auditing on source-validation segmentation change the no-target-label condition?

The audit uses source-validation segmentation, not target-domain labels. That keeps the audit reference distinct from the target-label restriction discussed for this approach. The activity does not specify the arrangements for obtaining LT-BackgroundFlip accuracy scores; it should not be taken as permission to use target labels to train or filter the adapters.
Can macro-accuracy be obtained without any reference for correct classes?

No. Computing accuracy requires a reference for whether predictions are correct. The activity says to score LT-BackgroundFlip tail and head macro-accuracy but does not describe the scoring arrangement. That omission should not be filled with an invented procedure, nor should it turn the no-target-label constraint into a claim that unlabeled predictions alone yield accuracy.
Suppose the audit finds high foreground retention. Could I then say the masks preserve the rare-class features that matter?

You could report the measured foreground retention once the audit has been done. High retained foreground area would not, by itself, prove that every recognition-relevant rare-class feature survived. The LT-BackgroundFlip accuracy comparison supplies additional evidence about recognition behavior, but it, too, should be reported only after scoring.
What is the most careful way to describe this activity right now?

Audit self-supervised mask retention against source-validation segmentation for the ≥90% foreground condition; train filtered and unfiltered adapters alongside an ERM baseline using identical training data; and score each condition’s tail and head macro-accuracy on LT-BackgroundFlip. This sets up an evaluation of the predicted gain and head-loss limit without asserting an audit result or an accuracy result.

The results are in: with 92% foreground retention, filtered swaps scored 35.1% tail macro-accuracy on LT-BackgroundFlip, compared with 32.0% for ERM. Head accuracy fell 0.6 points. How should I describe that?

Report the three observations together: foreground retention was 92%; on LT-BackgroundFlip, filtered swaps achieved 35.1% tail macro-accuracy versus 32.0% for empirical risk minimization (ERM), a difference of 3.1 percentage points; and head accuracy fell by 0.6 percentage points. That states the observed comparison without attributing the entire difference to any one component.
Is the tail difference 3.1% or 3.1 percentage points?
It is 3.1 percentage points: 35.1% minus 32.0%. Saying “3.1% higher” could be read as a relative increase, which is a different calculation.
Can I say the masks preserved 92% of the features needed to recognize rare classes?

No. The reported 92% is foreground retention, not a measurement of how many recognition-relevant features survived. A retained proportion of foreground does not identify which cues were kept. You can report the retention figure alongside the accuracy scores without treating those measurements as interchangeable.
Does the 35.1% figure describe all classes?

No. It is tail macro-accuracy on LT-BackgroundFlip for the filtered-swap condition. The 32.0% ERM figure is the corresponding tail macro-accuracy comparison. Neither number is stated as overall accuracy or as head macro-accuracy.
What can I say about the head result?
You can say that head accuracy fell by 0.6 percentage points. The evidence gives the size of that change, but not an absolute head accuracy value, so it would be inaccurate to supply one.
Do these numbers tell us whether filtering was better than leaving the swaps unfiltered?

Not from the figures given here. They report the filtered-swap tail score, the ERM tail score, foreground retention, and the head change. No unfiltered-swap accuracy is included, so this evidence does not quantify a filtered-versus-unfiltered difference.
Could I say the background swaps caused the 3.1-point tail difference?

The safe wording is that filtered swaps scored 3.1 percentage points above ERM on the reported tail macro-accuracy comparison. The figures alone do not isolate the effect of the background swaps from every other aspect of the filtered-swap condition.
Does the retention number explain why tail accuracy was higher?

It provides context for the scored condition: foreground retention was 92% when the filtered swaps produced the reported score. It does not, on its own, establish that retention caused the tail difference or show which retained object cues mattered.
